skill.name: Simile: what is compared, and why
skill.why: A simile helps you picture something by linking it to something you know.
skill.how: Find like or as. Name the two things. Ask what they share.

steps.say: Here's how I described the mangrove mud.

show.nudge: That's the thing I'm describing. What did I say it was like?
Like links the two things. What comes after it?

steps.ask: What is the mud compared to? Tap it.
steps.win: Yes! Mud is compared to pudding. The word like links them.

steps.say: Think like a painter. Read my next line too.
show: The mud was like chocolate pudding. My boots sank right in.
steps.ask: Why did I compare the mud to pudding?

options.text: The mud was soft and gooey.
The mud was sweet to eat.
options.reason: Mud isn't sweet, yuck! Read the next line. What did my boots do?

options.text: The mud was made of real chocolate.
options.reason: That's taking it literally, as if it's really true. It's mud, not pudding!

steps.win: Yes! Soft and gooey. Comparing with like or as is a simile.

steps.say: Careful! Zed says any sentence with as is a simile.
show: As soon as the bell rang, we ran to the boat.

check.nudge: Say it aloud. As soon as tells you when. Is anything said to be like something else?

steps.win: Right! As soon as tells you when. Nothing is compared.

options.text: I like chocolate pudding.
options.reason: Here like means enjoy. Nothing is compared to anything.

options.text: We ate treats like pudding and cake.
options.reason: Here like means such as. It's a list, not a comparison.

options.text: Mo's custard looked like wet cement.

steps.win: Yes! Custard is compared to wet cement. Lumpy and grey. Yum?

steps.say: Careful! Two kids the same height is a plain fact.

show.text: Tully is as tall as Mo.
show.nudge: Tully and Mo are both kids. That's just a fact about how tall they are.
Two kids again. It's a plain fact, with no picture in it.

show.text: Tully is as tall as a lamp post.

steps.ask: Tap the simile. Which one compares two different kinds of thing?
steps.win: Yes! A kid and a lamp post are different kinds of thing.

steps.say: Writers pick a simile that shows what they mean.
show: The old ferry crossed the bay ...
steps.ask: Which simile shows how slow the ferry was?

options.text: like a jet ski
options.reason: Jet skis zoom! Think of something that moves very slowly.

options.text: like a sleepy turtle
like a red fire engine
options.reason: A fire engine is red and loud. That's not about being slow.

steps.win: Yes! Sleepy turtles are slow. Ask what the two things share.

terms.means: Compares two different kinds of thing, using like or as.
The linking words. But 'as soon as' and 'I like' don't compare.
The different thing. Ask what the two things share.

card.test: Find like or as. Are two different kinds of thing compared? Ask what they share.

weDo.text: The egret stood on one leg in the shallow water. It was as still as a statue. It didn't even blink.
weDo.prompt: What is the egret compared to?
weDo.hint: Find the word as. What comes after 'as still as'?
weDo.success: A statue. 'As still as a statue' links the egret to something that never moves.

options.text: a statue
the water
options.reason: The egret stands in the water, but it isn't compared to it.

options.text: one leg
options.reason: Its leg is part of the egret. Look after 'as still as'.

weDo.hint: Find like. Is it comparing two different things?
weDo.success: The sandwich's smell is compared to old socks, using like. Pee-yew.

parts: Gus opened his lunchbox.

parts.tap: He likes cheese sandwiches best.
parts.reason: Here 'likes' means enjoys. Nothing is being compared.

parts.tap: The sandwich smelled like old socks.
He ate it anyway.
parts.reason: This just says what Gus did. There's no comparison.

creature.name: Likkaby
creature.blurb: A mudskipper that hops from one thing to another and links them with like or as. Catch it by asking what the two things share.

write.ask: Rewrite these as one sentence. Add a simile with like or as that shows how slow the blob was.
given: The green blob slid off Gus's bench.
write.starter: The green blob slid off Gus's bench
checks: I compared the blob to a different kind of thing.
My picture shows the blob was slow.
write.model: The green blob slid off Gus's bench as slowly as a snail climbing a wet window.

encounters.frame: A Likkaby is sitting on a soggy postcard it found in the mangrove roots.
encounters.text: Dear Nan, We went snorkelling at the reef today. The water was warm and clear. A huge turtle swam right under me. Its shell was as wide as our kitchen table. It didn't seem to mind me at all. It just munched on some seagrass and swam away slowly. Dad took a photo with his new camera, but his finger was over the lens. I'll draw it for you instead. Love, Kit

encounters.frame: A Likkaby hopped out of Zed's backpack with a page of his Space Camp diary.
encounters.text: Space Camp diary, Night 2. Tonight it was finally our turn on the big telescope. I had to stand on a milk crate to reach it. First we found the Moon. It was so bright and white that I had to squint. Its surface looked like the top of a crumpet. Our guide said the dents all over it were craters, punched out by space rocks. Then we found Saturn. It was much smaller than I expected, but I could see its rings! I wanted to stay all night. Then Jonah bumped the telescope with his elbow, and we spent ten minutes finding Saturn again. Best night ever.
encounters.prompt: Why does Zed compare the Moon to the top of a crumpet?
encounters.success: A crumpet's top is covered in little round holes. So is the Moon, thanks to its craters.

options.text: Both are a warm, golden-brown colour.
options.reason: Zed says the Moon was bright and white. What else does he notice on it?

options.text: Both look soft and squishy enough to eat.
options.reason: Nothing says the Moon looks soft. What does Zed see when he looks closely?

options.text: Both are covered in little round holes.

encounters.frame: This letter blew into the Soggy Biscuit. The Likkaby is reading over Gus's shoulder.
encounters.text: Dear RoboHome Shop, Last week I bought your Zoom-Clean robot vacuum. The box promised it would clean my whole house in ten minutes. It does not. It moves like a snail. It took two hours to cross the lounge room rug. It took all afternoon to reach the kitchen. By the time it got to the hallway, the dog had shed again. I will say this for it: the floor is spotless wherever it has been. It also never gets stuck under the couch. But I need a vacuum that finishes before bedtime. Please send me my money back, or a robot that actually zooms. Yours, Mrs Ada Fenn

encounters.frame: Mo is telling the crew about his last camping trip. The Likkaby has its fins over its ears.
encounters.text: Every night at camp, Grandpa fell asleep first. Then the snoring began. It started low and rumbly, like a truck waiting at the lights. Then it got louder and louder. The walls of our old green tent shook. A possum ran out of the tree above us. My little sister put her pillow over her head. Even the frogs by the creek went quiet. Mum tried poking Grandpa with a stick, but he just rolled over and kept going. In the morning, Grandpa said he had slept beautifully. 'Did anyone else hear that noise in the night?' he asked. We all just looked at him. Next time, Mum is bringing her phone to record it.
encounters.prompt: What is Grandpa's snoring compared to?
encounters.success: A truck waiting at the lights. 'Low and rumbly, like a truck' helps you hear it.

options.text: the frogs by the creek
options.reason: The frogs go quiet because of the noise. Nothing says the snoring is like them. Look after 'like'.

options.text: a truck waiting at the lights
the walls of our old green tent
options.reason: The tent walls shake from the noise, but the snoring isn't compared to them. Look after 'like'.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote this dive log after a night on the reef. The Likkaby is jealous it couldn't come.
encounters.text: Dive log, Tuesday. We dropped into the sunny shallows just after lunch, and within five minutes Tully spotted a cuttlefish hovering above the sand. It was about as long as my forearm, with a frilly fin running all the way around its body. At first it was a plain sandy brown, so it almost disappeared against the seafloor. Then it noticed us. Its skin flashed red, then white, then striped, then spotty, like a TV screen flicking through the channels. Gus was so surprised that he let out a cloud of bubbles. The cuttlefish didn't seem bothered. It drifted closer, waved two of its arms at Zed's mask, and turned a deep purple. Then, as quickly as it had arrived, it shot backwards and vanished into the seagrass. We searched for twenty minutes but never saw it again. Indi has already started a painting of it, though she says she'll need every colour she owns.
encounters.prompt: Why does Wren compare the cuttlefish's skin to a TV screen flicking through the channels?
encounters.success: Flicking channels makes the picture change fast. The cuttlefish's colours changed fast, one after another.

options.text: It glowed brightly, the way a screen does at night.
options.reason: The dive was in sunny shallows after lunch. What does a TV do when you flick channels?

options.text: Its colours changed quickly, one after another.
Its body was flat, with straight, square edges.
options.reason: Wren describes a frilly fin all round its body, not square edges. Think about flicking channels.

options.text: It was showing the crew pictures of the reef.
options.reason: That's taking it too literally. What happens on a screen when you flick channels?

encounters.frame: Tully is reading out a page from a bird-watcher's diary. The Likkaby is ducking.
encounters.text: Saturday, 6 am. I set up my folding chair on the boardwalk at low tide and waited for the mangrove kingfisher. The water in the channel was so still that it was like a mirror, and I could see every root reflected in it. A fisherman went past in a dinghy, and the ripples spread out behind him for ages. At half past six, I heard a sharp call above me. The kingfisher was sitting on a branch, its feathers as blue as a jewel in the early sun. It stared down at the water for a long time without moving. Then it tipped forward and dropped into the water like a thrown dart. There was a tiny splash. A second later, it was back on its branch with a crab in its beak, looking very pleased with itself. I was so excited that I knocked my thermos off the boardwalk. It's still down there somewhere.
encounters.prompt: The writer first wrote that the kingfisher dropped 'like a stone'. Why is 'like a thrown dart' a better fit?
encounters.success: Darts are aimed at a target. The kingfisher stared at the water, dived, and came back with a crab.

options.text: It dropped down towards the water very fast.
options.reason: A falling stone is fast too. What does a dart do that a dropped stone doesn't?

options.text: It aimed at one exact spot and hit its target.
It was heavy and hit the water with a big thump.
options.reason: That fits a stone. The diary says there was only a tiny splash.

options.text: Its blue feathers flashed brightly in the sun.
options.reason: That's the jewel simile's job. Darts and stones aren't about colour.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote a netball report for the crew. She's very proud of one simile.
encounters.text: The Reef Rays were down by two goals with a minute to play, and the ball was at the wrong end of the court. That's when Priya took over. She's the tallest player on our team, but she never seems to leave the ground, and she hardly says a word during a game. She grabbed the ball from their goal attack and turned. Then she darted between the defenders like a sparrow through the branches of a tree. Three players tried to block her, and not one of them got close enough to touch the ball. She passed to Jess, who passed to Ana, who scored. We won the centre pass, and Priya did it all again. When the final whistle blew, we had won by one goal. Priya just shrugged, tied her shoelace and asked if there were any orange slices left. Coach says it was the best minute of netball she has seen in thirty years of coaching.
encounters.prompt: What does the sparrow simile tell you about the way Priya moved?
encounters.success: Sparrows flit through branches without hitting them. Priya slipped quickly through the defenders, and nobody touched her.

options.text: She moved quickly, and the defenders couldn't stop her.
She jumped high into the air to catch the ball.
options.reason: Sparrows fly, but Tully says Priya never seems to leave the ground.

options.text: She was the smallest and lightest player on court.
options.reason: Sparrows are small, but Tully says Priya is the tallest player on the team.

options.text: She chatted and called out to her team the whole time.
options.reason: Sparrows chirp, but Tully says Priya hardly says a word during a game.

encounters.frame: Commander Rhee's log from the space station has been beamed to the Soggy Biscuit's radio.
encounters.text: Station log, day forty-one. This morning we passed over the middle of Australia just as the sun came up, and I floated by the window for the whole twelve minutes it took to cross. From four hundred kilometres up, the desert looked enormous and completely empty, a rusty brown that stretched from one edge of the window to the other. Then I spotted the river. It is one of the longest rivers on the continent, thousands of kilometres from end to end, yet from up here it wound across the desert like a loose thread dropped on a brown carpet. It was a thin, dark green line, curling back on itself again and again, and in places it almost disappeared. I tried to photograph it, but the camera kept focusing on a smudge where my nose had touched the glass. My crewmate Jo says I spend more time at the window than at my experiments. She is probably right. Tomorrow we pass over the reef, and I have already cleaned the glass. Jo has asked me to stop pressing my face against it, but I can't promise anything. The reef is meant to be the best view of the whole mission, and I don't intend to miss a second of it.
encounters.prompt: The river is thousands of kilometres long. Why does the commander still compare it to a loose thread?
encounters.success: A dropped thread looks thin and wiggly on a carpet. So did the river on the huge desert.

options.text: The river looked loose, as if it might drift off across the desert.
options.reason: Rivers stay put. A dropped thread is about shape, and the log says thin and curling.

options.text: The river looked short enough to pick up.
options.reason: That's too literal. The log says it's thousands of kilometres long. It only looked thin from so high.

options.text: The river looked thin and rusty brown, the same colour as the desert.
options.reason: Thin is right, but the log says the river was a dark green line, not brown.

options.text: The river looked thin and winding against the huge, empty desert.

encounters.frame: Gus's lab notebook is open on the galley table. The Likkaby has been told not to touch anything.
encounters.text: Experiment 14: the Mangrove Mud Monster. I mixed three cups of riverbank mud with glue, a sprinkle of borax and a spoonful of Mo's leftover gravy, which nobody else was going to eat. Then I strained out all the mud through one of Zed's socks. Within an hour, the mixture had become a single blob, so clear that I could read the ruler lying underneath it. When I poked it with a pencil, it stretched into long, gooey strings that took ages to snap. When I tilted the tray, the blob began to slide towards the edge. It moved so slowly that it took nearly ten minutes to reach the rim. Mo said it was the best gravy I had ever made. Now I need one simile for my report, so I have written four drafts. I want the one that fits everything I noticed about Kevin, which is what I have named the blob. Zed says I should pick the funniest one. I have told Zed that this is science, and that I still have his sock.
encounters.prompt: Tap the draft that fits everything Gus noticed about the blob.
encounters.success: Cold honey is slow, see-through and stringy. It's the only draft that matches all three things Gus noticed.

parts.reason: A turtle is slow, but you can't see through one, and it doesn't stretch into strings.

parts.reason: A raindrop is see-through, but it zips down fast and never stretches. Gus's blob took ten minutes.

parts.reason: Cement is slow and thick, but it's grey. You could read a ruler through Gus's blob.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote a note about Indi's gallery review. One word is wrong.
encounters.text: MIRAGE MANGROVES GALLERY: a review by Indi. The new exhibition, Tidelines, fills one long room with paintings of the mangroves at different times of day, and the first one stopped me in my tracks. It shows the channel at dawn. The artist has painted the mist as pale and delicate as tissue paper, so thin that the trees behind it show through, like shadows behind a curtain. In the next painting the tide is out, and the mudflats gleam like wet liquorice, dark and glossy, with crab holes dotted everywhere. A small sign beside it explains that the artist spent a whole winter on it. My favourite is the last painting, of the channel at night. The artist has used only black, deep blue and a few flecks of silver, and somehow it feels perfectly calm. I stood in front of it for ten minutes, and the gallery attendant asked if I was feeling all right. The only painting I didn't love was a giant portrait of Maxx Vantablack on his jet ski, which the gallery says he donated himself. Admission is free, so go before the exhibition closes at the end of the month. Bring a friend, and leave plenty of time for the night painting.

encounters.frame: Poet Pip has pinned this concert review to the Mirage Mangroves noticeboard.
encounters.text: The Mangrove Youth Orchestra played its end-of-year concert on Saturday night, in a tent pitched right on the edge of the mudflats. It was a bold choice of venue. Halfway through the first piece, the tide came in, and the cellists had to lift their feet onto their chairs. Nobody stopped playing. The highlight was a new piece called Storm Over the Channel, written by the orchestra's youngest member, a Year 6 student named Felix. It began with the violins playing so quietly that the notes were as faint as a mosquito in the next room. Slowly the drums joined in, and the whole tent seemed to tremble. By the final minute, the brass section was blasting out notes like foghorns across the bay, and a family of egrets took off from the trees in alarm. When the last note ended, there was a moment of complete silence. Then the audience burst into applause that drummed on and on, like heavy rain on a tin roof. Felix bowed three times and then, to everyone's delight, fell off the stage into the mud. The mud washed off his suit eventually, but the story will last a lot longer. He has already asked for three copies of this review.
encounters.prompt: The violins were 'as faint as a mosquito in the next room'. The brass was 'like foghorns across the bay'. What do the two similes show together?
encounters.success: A mosquito next door is barely heard. Foghorns blast. So the music built from a whisper to a roar.

options.text: Felix's piece was played right beside the water.
options.reason: The tent really was by the water, but these similes are about sound, not place.

options.text: The violins and the brass were both annoying to hear.
options.reason: Mosquitoes and foghorns can annoy you, but the reviewer loved the piece.

options.text: Felix's piece grew from almost silent to very loud.
The brass players were better than the violins.
options.reason: Neither simile says who played better. Each one shows how loud that part was.

encounters.prompt: Match each simile to what it tells you about the robot.
encounters.success: No clue words this time. Ask what each thing is known for, and which robot part it describes.

items.text: The Goldbot X was like a cheetah.
items.reason: Cheetahs are best known for their speed. So this robot is fast.

items.text: Its alarm was like a fire engine in a tunnel.
items.reason: A fire engine's siren in a tunnel is deafening, and it's the alarm being described.

items.text: Its armour was like a freshly polished mirror.
items.reason: A polished mirror gleams, and it's the armour being described.

items.text: The cargo robot was like a fridge stuck in a lift.
items.reason: A fridge in a lift fills the whole space. So this robot is huge.

items.text: The spy drone was like a swallow chasing midges.
items.reason: A swallow chasing insects darts about at speed. So the drone is fast.

items.text: The guard robot was like a block of flats on legs.
items.reason: A block of flats towers over you. So this robot is enormous.

items.text: Its visor was like sunlight on a swimming pool.
items.reason: Sunlight on a pool sparkles, and it's the visor being described.

encounters.frame: Maxx Vantablack is live-streaming a jet ski stunt. Zed is adding captions for the crew.
encounters.text: What's up, Vantafam! Maxx here, live from Green Screen Swamp, about to do the greatest jet ski jump in history. The ramp is made of three old pallets and a surfboard, and my stylist has sprayed my hair so it can't move. Ready? Here we go! The jet ski shot up the ramp and into the air, and so did Maxx. 'I flew off like a superhero!' he told his fans afterwards, while a pelican sat on his head. Zed watched the replay frame by frame. Maxx's arms flapped wildly. His legs pointed in two different directions. He turned over twice, then landed bottom-first in the mud with a heavy squelch and lay there for a while. Zed typed his own caption under the clip: 'Maxx flew off like a sack of potatoes.' Then he posted it to the crew chat. Tully laughed so hard that she dropped her toast in the sink. Maxx has asked his fans to report the caption, and to buy Maxx-Hold hairspray, only forty dollars a can. Two Xs, because one X is for losers.
encounters.prompt: What does Zed's 'like a sack of potatoes' show that Maxx's 'like a superhero' hides?
encounters.success: A sack of potatoes drops heavily and flops about. That matches the replay: flapping arms, two flips, a bottom-first landing.

options.text: Maxx flew a long way up into the air off the ramp.
options.reason: Superheroes fly too. What does a sack of potatoes do that a superhero doesn't?

options.text: Maxx was brave enough to try a dangerous stunt.
options.reason: That's what Maxx wants 'like a superhero' to show. A sack of potatoes isn't brave.

options.text: Maxx fell heavily and clumsily, with no control at all.
Maxx was carrying heavy shopping on the jet ski.
options.reason: That's taking it too literally. Nothing says Maxx had any shopping with him.
